video_script.design: One idea: the new square must be a square and exactly double. Assumes: area as the ground a shape covers. maths_rules: About 800 BCE: 800 + 2026 = 2826 years before today, said as about two thousand eight hundred years ago.
Baudhāyana wrote the Śulba Sūtra, c. 800 BCE; in it he asks how to construct a square having double the area of a given square.
A square has four equal sides and four square corners. Its area is its side times its side.
The book's first guess is to double the length of each side; it is said once here and left open, never drawn and never tested.
The last frame is a 9 by 9 grid of dots, one unit apart, holding the given square of side 2 units, area 2 x 2 = 4 square units, with the words square and exactly double beside it.
Exactly double would be 8 square units; this number is never shown or said.
video_script.substitution: Any idea must pass two tests: the new shape is a square, and its area is exactly double.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: the new square must pass two tests, it must be a square and its area must be exactly double. The book's first guess, making every side twice as long, is left unbroken on purpose; the next topic counts it.

content.text:
About 800 BCE, Baudhāyana wrote the Śulba-Sūtra. In it he asks how to construct a square having double the area of a given square.
A square has four equal sides and four square corners, and its area is its side times its side.
The new shape must still be a square, and its area must be exactly double.
This one question leads through the whole chapter: doubling, halving and combining squares, a length known by its area before it is known as a number, whole-number right triangles, a puzzle that took more than 300 years to prove, and a lotus in a lake.

media.description: Two blue squares sit side by side. The left square has corner vertices labelled "A", "B", "C", and "D", a solid blue fill, and a tick mark on its bottom and right sides. A label underneath reads "AB = 1 unit". The right square has corner vertices labelled "E", "F", "G", and "H", with two tick marks on its bottom side and two on its left side. One horizontal dashed line and one vertical dashed line cut it into four equal pale blue square cells. Below it, a label reads "EF = 2 units".

media.teaching_notes: Ask the student to count the dashed cells. Then ask: if 4 copies fit, what fraction of the big square is one copy? This fixes the idea that doubling the side is too much.

media.generation_prompt:
MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: Doubling the side of a square gives 4 times the area: 4 copies of the original square exactly fill the square with doubled side.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: teal #0072B2 for the first set, amber #E69F00 for the second set, green #009E73 for what agrees or works, reddish purple #CC79A7 for the focus, grey #6B7280 for construction; muted red #D55E00 only for a wrong or impossible case, never as decoration. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. Two squares side by side on a white background, bottoms level. Left: the original square, small, teal fill. Right: the square with doubled side, exactly twice the side length of the left square, drawn with a solid outline and split by one dashed horizontal line and one dashed vertical line through its centre into 4 equal cells; each cell has a light teal fill so each reads as a copy of the left square. Tick marks at the middle of the sides show equal lengths: one tick on the left square's bottom side and right side, and one tick on each half of the big square's bottom side and left side.

Exact mathematical structure:
- Left square: side 1 unit, a true square.
- Right square: side 2 units, exactly twice the left square's side, a true square.
- The right square has exactly 1 dashed horizontal line and exactly 1 dashed vertical line, both through its centre.
- The dashed lines make exactly 4 equal cells, each the same size as the left square.
- Each half of the right square's bottom side and left side carries 1 tick mark, matching the tick on the left square.

Visible text:
- side 1 unit
- side 2 units
- 1 square unit
- 4 square units

Critical rejection conditions:
- the right square's side anything other than exactly twice the left square's side
- a number of dashed cells other than 4, or cells of unequal size
- either square drawn as a rectangle
- any label saying the big square is double the area
- any count of objects, cells, ticks or dots that differs from the numbers stated above
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
- a right angle drawn visibly different from 90 degrees, or a right-angle mark on a corner that is not a right angle

Student takeaway: Double the side and count: 4 copies of the original fit inside, so 4 times the area, not double.

MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: The square with double the area is built with the diagonal of the original square as its side, standing tilted on that diagonal.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: teal #0072B2 for the first set, amber #E69F00 for the second set, green #009E73 for what agrees or works, reddish purple #CC79A7 for the focus, grey #6B7280 for construction; muted red #D55E00 only for a wrong or impossible case, never as decoration. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. The original square, upright, in the lower left of the frame, solid outline with a teal fill. One diagonal runs from its top-left corner to its bottom-right corner, drawn as a reddish purple line. A tilted square (a square standing on one corner, like a diamond) is built outward on this diagonal, away from the original square's bottom-left corner, drawn with a dashed outline and a light amber fill. Its top vertex sits directly above the original square's top-right corner and its right vertex sits directly to the right of that same corner.

Exact mathematical structure:
- Place the original square with corners at (0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1) and (0, 1).
- The diagonal joins (0, 1) and (1, 0).
- The tilted square has vertices (0, 1), (1, 0), (2, 1) and (1, 2): its side is the diagonal.
- The tilted square's centre is the original square's top-right corner (1, 1).
- The tilted square is a true square: 4 equal sides and 4 right angles, 1 small right-angle square mark at the vertex (1, 2).
- Only one diagonal is drawn in the original square.

Visible text:
- original square
- diagonal
- square on the diagonal

Critical rejection conditions:
- the tilted square built on a side of the original square instead of its diagonal
- the tilted square drawn as a rhombus with unequal angles, or not sharing the whole diagonal as a side
- the tilted square overlapping the lower-left half of the original square
- any east-west or north-south lines inside the tilted square (they belong to the next concept)
- any count of objects, cells, ticks or dots that differs from the numbers stated above
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
- a right angle drawn visibly different from 90 degrees, or a right-angle mark on a corner that is not a right angle

media.description: A square has side 1 unit, and a new square has every side doubled. A common slip says two of the small squares will fill it. Lines across and down split the new square into cells the size of the small square. How many small squares fill it?

video_script.why: Doubling the side feels like it should double the area. How many times the area does it really give?

maths_rules: Old square: corners (0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1), (0, 1). Its diagonal joins (0, 1) and (1, 0). The dotted square has corners (0, 1), (1, 0), (2, 1), (1, 2).
The diagonal cuts the old square into 2 triangles: (0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1) and (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1).

The north-south line is the right side of the old square carried on from (1, 1) up to (1, 2), the top corner of the dotted square. The east-west line is the top side carried on from (1, 1) to (2, 1), the right corner.
These lines cut the dotted square into 4 triangles: (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1) (shared with the old square), (0, 1), (1, 1), (1, 2), (1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1) and (1, 0), (2, 1), (1, 1).
Every one of these triangles has a right angle and two sides of 1 unit; a copy of the shared triangle, turned, covers each outside triangle exactly.
Old square = 2 triangles, dotted square = 4 triangles; 4 = 2 x 2, so the dotted square has double the area (1 and 2 square units).
Your turn: 12 of these triangles; 2 triangles make 1 square of side 1 unit, so 12 / 2 = 6 squares of side 1 unit, never shown or said.

maths_rules: Square 1 and Square 2 are identical: side s, drawn the same size. Square 1: corners (0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1), (0, 1) with s = 1.
Square 1 stays whole; its two diagonals mark triangles 1 (left), 2 (top), 3 (right), 4 (bottom), each with its square corner at the centre (0.5, 0.5), as in the book's figure.
Square 2 is cut along both diagonals into pieces 5 (left), 6 (top), 7 (right), 8 (bottom), each with its long side on a side of Square 2 and its square corner at the centre.
A square's diagonals are equal, cut each other in half and meet at right angles, and the two squares are identical, so all 8 triangles are congruent.
The slip's check: pieces 5 to 8 pushed back together make Square 2 again, exactly its old size.

Placing (each piece only slides, none turns): piece 7 against the left side of Square 1, square corner at (-0.5, 0.5); piece 8 against the top side, square corner at (0.5, 1.5); piece 5 against the right side, square corner at (1.5, 0.5); piece 6 against the bottom side, square corner at (0.5, -0.5).
At each corner of Square 1, two 45 degree corners of pieces meet its 90 degree corner: 45 + 90 + 45 = 180 degrees, so the outline runs straight on through that corner.

The outline has corners (1.5, 0.5), (0.5, 1.5), (-0.5, 0.5), (0.5, -0.5). Each side is two short sides of pieces, so all four sides are equal; each corner is a piece's 90 degree corner. It is a square standing on a corner.
New square = 4 triangles of Square 1 + 4 pieces = 8 congruent triangles; Square 1 = 4; 8 / 4 = 2, so double the area (2 square units against 1).
Your turn: squares of side 6 cm; Square 1 has area 6 x 6 = 36 square cm; the new square has 2 x 36 = 72 square cm. Never shown or said.

maths_rules: Old square: corners (0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1), (0, 1), side 1 unit; its diagonal joins (0, 1) and (1, 0). Dotted square: corners (0, 1), (1, 0), (2, 1), (1, 2), centre (1, 1).
Right angles: T1 at (0, 0); T2, T3, T4 and T5 at (1, 1). Each is where an east-west line meets a north-south line.
Sides beside the right angle: T1 and T2 use sides of the old square, 1 unit each.

The carried lines x = 1 (from (1, 0) to (1, 2)) and y = 1 (from (0, 1) to (2, 1)) are the dotted square's diagonals. A square's diagonals are equal and cut each other in half, so the four halves from the centre (1, 1) are equal. Two of them, (1, 1) to (1, 0) and (1, 1) to (0, 1), are sides of the old square, 1 unit, so every half is 1 unit.
So T3, T4 and T5 each have two sides of 1 unit with a right angle between them, like T1 and T2. By the side angle side rule all five are congruent.
The slip's check: T3 turned a quarter turn clockwise about (1, 1) lands exactly on T4.

maths_rules: Old square: corners (0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1), (0, 1); its diagonal joins (0, 1) and (1, 0). Dotted square: corners (0, 1), (1, 0), (2, 1), (1, 2).

A square's diagonal cuts each of its 90 degree corners into 45 + 45 degrees, and the line from a corner that cuts it into two equal halves is the diagonal, which reaches the opposite corner (the book's hint, the diagonal property of a square).
At (1, 0), the bottom corner of the dotted square, the corner is 90 degrees, between its sides towards (0, 1) and towards (2, 1).

The old square's right side leaves (1, 0) straight up. It makes 45 degrees with the diagonal (towards (0, 1)); 90 - 45 = 45 degrees remain to the side towards (2, 1). It cuts the corner into 45 + 45: it bisects it.
The line through (1, 0) that bisects the dotted square's corner there is the dotted square's diagonal, so it reaches the opposite corner (1, 2): the carried right side passes through (1, 2).
At (0, 1), the top side leaves straight right; it makes 45 degrees with the diagonal (towards (1, 0)) and 45 degrees with the side towards (1, 2), so it bisects that corner and reaches (2, 1).
The slip's picture: a line drawn slightly off the corner, missing it; it is shown only to fail and is struck.
Your turn: a line leaves a 90 degree corner of a square at 30 degrees to one side; 30 is not 45, so it does not bisect the corner and misses the opposite corner. Never shown or said.

video_script.design: One idea: count congruent triangles, 4 out of 8. Assumes: the doubling sequence of 2, 4 and 8 triangles. Wrong idea: the slip judges size by the corners touching the sides. maths_rules: Big square: corners (0, 0), (2, 0), (2, 2), (0, 2). Midpoints of its sides: (1, 0), (2, 1), (1, 2), (0, 1).
The inside square joins (1, 0), (2, 1), (1, 2), (0, 1) in order; it stands on a corner. It is the doubling picture run backwards: the inside square plays the part of the square on the diagonal.
The east-west line joins (0, 1) and (2, 1); the north-south line joins (1, 0) and (1, 2). They cut the big square into 4 equal small upright squares of side 1.
Each side of the inside square runs corner to corner across one small square, cutting it into 2 congruent triangles. The 4 small squares are equal, so all 8 triangles are congruent.
Big square = 4 x 2 = 8 triangles. The inside square holds 4 of them, one from each small square; the 4 corner triangles lie outside it.
4 is half of 8, so the inside square has half the area of the big square (2 square units against 4).
The slip: judging by the corners touching the sides; the 4 corner pieces outside are whole triangles, together as big as the inside square.
Your turn: a square of area 18 square units; the square joining its midpoints has 18 / 2 = 9 square units. Never shown or said.

final_answer.value: 4 triangles out of 8, so half the area

media.title: Halving a Square
media.context: Class 8 'The Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem', 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 exercises. The construction tool of the concept 'Halving a square': the student builds the midpoint square step by step, then checks that it is a square with half the area. It sits on the halving concept, after its explanation and before the practice concept. The tool was built by the user as standalone HTML (Tools/halving_a_square/halving-a-square.html); the TSX port keeps this reserved url.
media.description: Students construct a square with half the area of a given square through an interactive, step-by-step construction rather than being shown the completed answer. They first mark the midpoint of each side, then fold the four corners towards the centre to form the inner figure PQRS. Students investigate whether PQRS is a square by checking its side lengths and angles, join its diagonals, compare the congruent triangles, and finally verify that PQRS contains 4 of the 8 equal triangles of the original square. The tool allows students to make and correct their own construction, use hints when needed, and verify the final area relationship.

tool_config.doer: Mark the midpoint of each side of a paper square and fold the four corners to the centre. Name the shape PQRS you get, then check its sides and angles, join its diagonals, match the congruent triangles and compare the areas. Use a hint when you need one, and undo any move.
tasks: Mark the four midpoints and fold the four corners to the centre.
Name the shape PQRS, then check its four sides and four angles.
Join the diagonals of PQRS and match the congruent triangles.
Compare the areas: PQRS is 4 of the paper's 8 congruent triangles.

video_script.anchor: Why is PQRS a square? Why is its area half the paper?
video_script.design: One idea: name the triangles, match them, count. Assumes: midpoints and the side angle side rule. Wrong idea: the slip judges a square by how it stands. Transitions: the folded paper stays from the hook to the end of the idea part; QS and PR are added in the ground part; one hard clear before the recap.
source: Book question: Fold the corners inward so the creases pass through the midpoints of t
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip says PQRS stands on a corner, so it is not a square; the paper is turned an eighth of a turn and PQRS sits upright, with the same sides and corners
maths_rules: Paper: corners (0, 0), (2, 0), (2, 2), (0, 2), side 2 units; centre (1, 1). Midpoints as in the book's figure: P (1, 0) bottom, Q (2, 1) right, R (1, 2) top, S (0, 1) left.

Folding corner (2, 0) onto the centre (1, 1) makes a crease along the line through P (1, 0) and Q (2, 1); the other three corners fold along QR, RS and SP. The four flaps meet at the centre with no gap and no overlap.
QS joins (2, 1) and (0, 1) (east-west); PR joins (1, 0) and (1, 2) (north-south). They cross at the centre at a right angle, and each half is 1 unit, half the paper's side.

Triangles P, Q, centre; Q, R, centre; R, S, centre; S, P, centre: each has two sides of 1 unit at the centre with a right angle between them, so they are congruent by side angle side; PQ = QR = RS = SP.

Each of these triangles has two equal sides, so its other two angles are equal: 90 + 2 x 45 = 180, each 45 degrees. Angle SPQ = 45 + 45 = 90 degrees; the same at Q, R and S. Four equal sides and four right angles: PQRS is a square.
Each folded flap, e.g. corner (2, 0) with P and Q, has a right angle between two sides of 1 unit, and the fold lays it exactly on triangle P, Q, centre: congruent.
Paper = 4 corner triangles + 4 triangles of PQRS = 8 congruent triangles; PQRS = 4 of 8 = half (2 square units against 4).
The slip's check: an eighth of a turn (45 degrees) sets PQRS upright; turning changes no side and no corner.
Your turn: paper of side 14 cm, area 14 x 14 = 196 square cm; PQRS has 196 / 2 = 98 square cm. Never shown or said.
video_script.payoff_line: P Q R S is four of the paper's eight congruent triangles, so it has half the area.

final_answer.value: PQRS has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles, so it is a square; it is 4 of the paper's 8 congruent triangles, so it has half the area
final_answer.spoken: four of the paper's eight congruent triangles

video_script.substitution: QS and PR cut the paper's centre into four congruent right triangles; they give equal sides and square corners, and each folded flap is one more such triangle.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: name the triangles, match them by side angle side, then count. Watch for students who say a square standing on a corner is not a square; how a shape stands never changes its sides or corners.

interaction_points.answer: PQRS has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles, so it is a square; it is 4 of the paper's 8 congruent triangles, so it has half the area

2. New side = 2 units.
3. New area = 2 × 2 = 4 square units.
4. 4 copies of the original square fill the new square.
Answer: 4 times the area, not double

content.text:
Why does the new dotted square have double the area of the original square?
In many of the constructions in the Śulba-Sūtra, it is desirable to construct, where needed, what Baudhāyana calls 'east-west' and 'north-south' lines, i.e., horizontal and vertical lines that are perpendicular to each other. Can you draw some horizontal and vertical lines to see why the new square has double the area of the original square?
You could draw some horizontal and vertical lines as shown on the right.
Why should the extension of the vertical and horizontal sides of the original square pass through the vertices of the dotted square?
[Hint: From the diagonal property of a square, the line that bisects an angle passes through the opposite vertex. Argue why the vertical and horizontal sides of the original square bisect the two angles of the dotted square.]
So, the new square has double the area of the original square, because the original square is made up of two small triangles, while the new square is made up of four small triangles.
Moreover, all these small triangles are congruent to each other. Can you explain why?
Adding some more horizontal and vertical lines can make the situation even clearer:
So we can make the following sequence of squares:
Each square has double the area of the previous one, as they are made up of 2, 4, and 8 small triangles, respectively.

Now place the pieces 5, 6, 7, and 8 around Square 1 to get a square with double the area.

content.text:
Why should the extension of the vertical and horizontal sides of the original square pass through the vertices of the dotted square?
1. The diagonal of the original square makes 45° with each side of the original square.
2. At an end of the diagonal, the dotted square has a 90° corner.
3. The side of the original square at that end makes 45° with the diagonal, so it splits the 90° corner into 45° and 45°: it bisects the angle of the dotted square.
4. In a square, the line that bisects an angle is a diagonal, and it passes through the opposite vertex.
5. So the extended vertical side passes through the far vertex of the dotted square; the horizontal side does the same at the other end of the diagonal.
Answer: The extended sides bisect the dotted square's angles, so they are its diagonals and pass through its vertices

concepts.concept_description: Students investigate how to obtain a square with exactly half the area of a given square. First, they explore why simply halving the side of a square does not produce half the area; it produces one-quarter of the area. They then identify the midpoints of the four sides and construct the square formed by joining these midpoints. By examining the resulting triangles, equal sides, and right angles, students verify that the midpoint figure is a square and that it occupies exactly half of the original square. This connects halving directly to the earlier doubling construction as the reverse relationship.

content.text:
Fold the corners inward so the creases pass through the midpoints of the sides. Why is PQRS a square, and why is its area half that of the original paper?
1. P, Q, R and S are the midpoints of the sides of the paper.
2. Join QS and PR: they cross at the centre of the paper at right angles.
3. The four triangles around the centre, such as the one with vertices P, Q and the centre, each have two sides equal to half the side of the paper and a right angle between them, so they are congruent.
4. So PQ = QR = RS = SP.
5. Each of these right triangles has two equal sides, so its other two angles are 45° each; each angle of PQRS, such as angle SPQ, is 45° + 45°, a right angle.
6. Four equal sides and four right angles: PQRS is a square.
7. Each folded corner is congruent to the triangle it covers, so the paper is 8 triangles and PQRS is 4 of them: half.
Answer: PQRS has four equal sides and four right angles, so it is a square; it is 4 of the paper's 8 congruent triangles, so it has half the area

Isosceles Right Triangles, Q1: Earlier, we saw a method to create a square with double the area of a given square paper. There is another method to do this in which two identical square papers are cut in the following way: each square is cut along one diagonal, into pieces 1 and 2, and 3 and 4. Can you arrange these pieces to create a square with double the area of either square?
1. Each square is cut along one diagonal into 2 congruent right triangles: 4 triangles in all.
2. Each triangle has two sides equal to the side of the square, with a right angle between them.
3. Put the four right angles together at one point: four right angles fill the full turn around it with no gap.
4. The four long sides, each a diagonal of the square, form the outside: a square whose side is the diagonal.
5. It is made of the 4 triangles of two squares, so its area is double either square.
Answer: Yes: put the four right-angle corners together at the centre; the four diagonals make a square with double the area

topic_objective.objective_text: Students test their tries at doubling against counts: doubling a square's side gives four times the area, the square on the diagonal gives exactly double and the midpoint square exactly half, and congruent triangles keep their area when moved. Doubling and halving are the first steps to combining any two squares.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students check their own tries against a count, finding that the square with doubled side holds 4 copies of the original, and draw the square on the diagonal that Baudhāyana gives for exactly double the area.
Students draw east-west and north-south lines to split both squares into congruent triangles, explain why the diagonal square holds 4 of them against 2, and extend the pattern to 2, 4 and 8.

Students construct the square joining the midpoints of a given square, verify that it has four equal sides and four right angles, and use congruent triangles to establish that its area is exactly half of the original square.
Students rearrange triangles cut from two identical squares into one square of double area, in two different ways, and explain from triangle counts why the area stays the same while the pieces move.

video_script.design: One idea: count copies of the triangle, two against four. Assumes: area of a square is side times side, and the hypotenuse faces the right angle. video_script.wrong_move: A common slip lays the two equal sides end to end along the hypotenuse and says c is two eigh; the two sides overshoot the fold, because going round the corner is longer than the straight fold.
maths_rules: triangle PQS: right angle at P, PQ = PS = a, hypotenuse SQ = c; drawn with P bottom left, Q bottom right, S top left
a second copy turned half a turn about the midpoint of SQ fills SRQ; PQRS is a square of side a, area a x a = a^2, made of exactly 2 copies
V is a distance a to the right of R, level with S and R; U is a distance a straight above R
RS = RQ = RV = RU = a and the lines SV and QU cross at R at right angles, so SRQ, QRV, VRU and URS are 4 copies of the triangle
SQVU is the square on SQ, side c, area c x c = c^2, made of exactly 4 copies
4 copies = 2 x (2 copies), so c^2 = 2 x a^2 = 2a^2; taking the square root, c = a x root 2, because (a x root 2)^2 = a^2 x 2
The slip's c = 2a is false: the path S to P to Q has length a + a = 2a and the straight segment SQ is shorter
your turn: equal sides 11, square on the hypotenuse 2 x 11^2 = 2 x 121 = 242, never shown

video_script.anchor: Is the square on the hypotenuse always double the square on an equal side?
video_script.design: One idea: four copies make a true square on the hypotenuse, two copies make the square on a side. Assumes: angles of a triangle add to 180, area of a square. Wrong idea: a common slip takes the bottom side of a turned triangle as the hypotenuse. The grid stays through the ground and break; one clear before the proof, where the figure PQS stays all through the idea part; one clear before the recap.
source: The rule c² = 2a² for every isosceles right triangle
never_show: the bottom side labelled as the hypotenuse, except struck through
800, the answer to the closing question
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip turns the triangle onto its corner, calls the bottom side the hypotenuse and builds the square there; that side touches the right angle, so it is an equal side and its square is not double.
maths_rules: the picture is a grid of unit squares; each unit square has area 1

case 1: equal sides 1 unit, P(0,0), Q(1,0), S(0,1); square on a side = 1 square unit; square on SQ has corners S(0,1), Q(1,0), V(2,1), U(1,2); the grid lines through R(1,1) cut it into 4 half squares, area 4 x 1/2 = 2 square units = 2 x 1

case 2: equal sides 2 units, P(0,0), Q(2,0), S(0,2); square on a side = 2 x 2 = 4 square units; square on SQ has corners S(0,2), Q(2,0), V(4,2), U(2,4); it holds 4 triangles, each 1 whole square + 2 half squares = 2 square units, so 8 square units = 2 x 4
the slip's turned triangle: the side on the ground touches the right angle, so it is an equal side, not the hypotenuse
Given: triangle PQS, right angle at P, PQ = PS = a, SQ = c. To prove: c^2 = 2a^2
the angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees; the right angle is 90, so the two equal angles at Q and S are 45 each
a copy turned half a turn about the midpoint of SQ gives triangle SRQ; at S and at Q a 45 meets a 45, making 90; so PQRS has 4 sides a and 4 right angles: a square, area a^2, made of 2 copies
Construction: extend SR past R by a to V, and QR past R by a to U; RS = RQ = RV = RU = a
SRV and QRU are straight lines and angle SRQ = 90, so all four angles at R are 90
triangles SRQ, QRV, VRU, URS each have two sides a with a right angle between them, so each is a copy of PQS; their long sides SQ, QV, VU, US are each c
each corner of SQVU is 45 + 45 = 90, so SQVU is a square of side c, area c^2, made of 4 copies
4 copies = 2 x 2 copies, so c^2 = 2 x a^2 = 2a^2 for every length a
closing question: equal sides 20, square on the hypotenuse 2 x 20^2 = 2 x 400 = 800, never shown

final_answer.value: c² = 2a²
final_answer.spoken: c squared equals two eigh squared

media.title: Equal sides of 12: how long is the hypotenuse?
media.context: Class 8 'The Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem'. Worked video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea.
media.description: A right triangle has two equal sides of 12 units. The video asks how long the hypotenuse is, tests a common slip of adding the sides, and builds the answer step by step.

video_script.why: How do you find the hypotenuse from the equal sides when the answer is not a whole number?

<bookmark mark='pin'/>Two hundred and eighty eight sits between sixteen squared and seventeen squared. That means it is not a whole number, and c is between sixteen and seventeen units.
<bookmark mark='close'/>It is very close to seventeen, and far from twenty four.

source: Example 1

media.title: Does c² = 2a² agree with adding the areas of two squares?
media.context: Class 8 'The Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem'. Worked video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea.
media.description: Two triangles are checked with the rule that links the equal sides and the hypotenuse. The video tests a common slip, then reads the rule forwards and backwards.

<bookmark mark='one'/>First, the hypotenuse when the equal sides are three. <bookmark mark='two'/>Second, each equal side when the hypotenuse is ten.

<bookmark mark='second'/>In the second we know the hypotenuse, so square it, halve it, and take the root.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>It is one rule, read in two directions.

<bookmark mark='tick'/>That matches adding the areas: three squared plus three squared is eighteen.

<bookmark mark='trap'/>Seven squared is forty nine, so it is a little over seven.
<bookmark mark='same'/>The rule gives root eighteen and root fifty, the same answers that adding the areas gives.
<bookmark mark='note'/>In your notebook, write double when you go forwards, and halve when you go back.

<bookmark mark='yours'/>Your turn. Find the hypotenuse when the equal sides are sixteen. Then find each equal side when the hypotenuse is fourteen.

video_script.anchor: Check with c² = 2a²: equal sides 3, and hypotenuse 10
video_script.design: One idea: the same rule, read forwards and backwards, gives the same answers as adding the areas. Assumes: c² = 2a² and squaring whole numbers. Wrong idea: forgetting to halve. The two triangles stay side by side from the ground to the idea; one clear before the recap.
source: Book question: Use c² = 2a² to check two earlier answers: the hypotenuse for equal si
video_script.wrong_move: The slip squares the hypotenuse 10 and takes the root without halving, so each side comes out 10, as long as the hypotenuse; a side can never be as long as the hypotenuse.
maths_rules: triangle 1: equal sides a = 3; c^2 = 2 x 3^2 = 2 x 9 = 18, so c = √18; 4^2 = 16 and 5^2 = 25, so 4 < √18 < 5, the same as adding the areas of two squares, 9 + 9 = 18
triangle 2: hypotenuse c = 10; c^2 = 10 x 10 = 100; 2a^2 = 100, so a^2 = 100 ÷ 2 = 50 and a = √50; 7^2 = 49 and 8^2 = 64, so 7 < √50 < 8, the same as adding the areas, 50 + 50 = 100
The slip skips the halving: √100 = 10 would make each side equal to the hypotenuse, but the hypotenuse is the longest side
your turn: equal sides 16, c^2 = 2 x 256 = 512, c = √512, 22^2 = 484 and 23^2 = 529 so 22 < √512 < 23; hypotenuse 14, 14^2 = 196, a^2 = 98, a = √98; never shown
video_script.payoff_line: The rule gives root eighteen and root fifty, the same answers that adding the areas gives

final_answer.spoken: root eighteen and root fifty

video_script.substitution: From a side: square, double, root. From the hypotenuse: square, halve, root.

media.teaching_notes: One rule, read in two directions: double when you start from a side, halve when you start from the hypotenuse. Watch for a child who forgets to halve and gets a side as long as the hypotenuse.

media.title: The hypotenuse is √72: how long are the other two sides?
media.context: Class 8 'The Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem'. Worked video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea.
media.description: A square folded corner to corner has a fold of root 72 units. The video works the rule backwards to find the equal sides, tests a common slip about halving, and checks the answer.

video_script.why: How do you go back from the hypotenuse to the equal sides?

narration: <bookmark mark='ex'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='fold'/>A paper square is folded from one corner to the opposite corner.
<bookmark mark='hyp'/>The fold is the hypotenuse, and it measures root seventy two units.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How long is each of the other two sides of the triangle?

<bookmark mark='moves'/>Read the rule backwards: square the hypotenuse, halve it, then take the root.
One fact helps first. <bookmark mark='nine'/>Root nine is three, because three times three is nine.
<bookmark mark='undo'/>Multiply root nine by itself, and you get nine again.

<bookmark mark='bar'/>A side of thirty six would be far longer than the fold itself.
The hypotenuse is the longest side, so that cannot be right.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>That stops too early, because thirty six is the area of a square, not a side.

<bookmark mark='half'/>Halve it, and eigh squared is thirty six square units.
<bookmark mark='root'/>Six times six is thirty six. That means each of the other two sides is six units long.

marks.note: the notebook lines appear one per line

<bookmark mark='long'/>Eight squared is sixty four and nine squared is eighty one. That puts root seventy two between eight and nine, so the fold is longer than six.
<bookmark mark='note'/>In your notebook, write square, halve and root, each on its own line.

marks.yours: the new triangle with hypotenuse √392 appears

video_script.anchor: Hypotenuse √72: how long is each equal side?
video_script.design: One idea: read the rule backwards, square, halve, root. Assumes: c² = 2a² and that squaring undoes a root. Wrong idea: stopping at the area 36. The folded square stays on stage from the hook to the idea; one clear before the recap.
source: Example 2
video_script.wrong_move: The slip is to halve 72 to get 36 and stop, calling 36 the side; a side of 36 would be far longer than the hypotenuse, which is between 8 and 9.
maths_rules: the folded square is an isosceles right triangle; the fold is the hypotenuse c = √72 units; the two equal sides a are unknown
√9 = 3 and 3^2 = 9, so squaring undoes a square root: (√72)^2 = 72
8^2 = 64 and 9^2 = 81, so 8 < √72 < 9; the hypotenuse is the longest side, and 6 < 8
The slipped 36 is a^2, the area of the square on a side in square units; a side of 36 would be longer than the hypotenuse
your turn: hypotenuse √392; 392 ÷ 2 = 196 and 14 x 14 = 196, so each side is 14; never shown
video_script.payoff_line: each of the other two sides is six units long

final_answer.value: Each of the other two sides has length 6
final_answer.spoken: six units each

video_script.substitution: Square the hypotenuse, halve it, then take the root.

media.teaching_notes: From c: square, halve, then take the root. Watch for the learner who stops at 36: that is the area of the square on a side, not the side, and a side of 36 would be longer than the hypotenuse.

interaction_points.answer: Each of the other two sides has length 6

media.description: A square with sides of 5 cm is cut corner to corner. The video asks how long the cut is, tests a common slip of adding two sides, and uses a hint for each step.

<bookmark mark='square'/>Here is a square, five centimetres on each side.
<bookmark mark='cut'/>A cut runs from one corner to the opposite corner. How long is the cut, the diagonal of the square?

marks.stop: the question mark on the cut is underlined in the accent colour

<bookmark mark='corner'/>Each one has a square corner, with two sides of five centimetres.
<bookmark mark='hyp'/>The cut faces that corner, so it is the hypotenuse.
<bookmark mark='want'/>We know each equal side, and we want c. Try again with this.

beats.colours: the slipped path = warning, diagonal = hypotenuse
narration: [chintu] <bookmark mark='slipsay'/>A common slip: five plus five, so the cut is ten centimetres.
<bookmark mark='round'/>Ten centimetres is the walk around two edges.
<bookmark mark='straight'/>Laid end to end along the cut, those two edges stick out past it, so they are longer.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>Adding the sides does not give the diagonal.

<bookmark mark='root'/>Take the root. The diagonal is root fifty centimetres.

content.text:
General Solution
The relation between the areas of a square and the square on its diagonal can be used to find a general relation between the hypotenuse and the other two sides of an isosceles right triangle.
Let a be the length of the equal sides and c the length of the hypotenuse.
Area of SQVU = 2 × Area of PQRS. So, c² = 2a².
This formula can be used to find c when a is known, or to find a when c is known.

content.text: An isosceles right triangle has equal sides 5. Without drawing: will the square on its hypotenuse have area 10, 25 or 50?

content.text:
Take any isosceles right triangle PQS with equal sides a and hypotenuse SQ = c.
Two copies make the square PQRS with side a, so its area is a².
SQ is the diagonal of PQRS, and the square SQVU on it has double the area: c² = 2a².
For equal sides 5: 2 × 5² = 2 × 25 = 50, so the square on the hypotenuse has area 50.
Read c² = 2a² both ways: from a, square, double, then take the root; from c, square, halve, then take the root.

content.text:
Show that c² = 2a² for an isosceles right triangle with equal sides a and hypotenuse c.
1. Two copies of the triangle make the square PQRS with side a.
2. Area of PQRS = a × a = a².
3. The hypotenuse SQ is the diagonal of PQRS.
4. The square SQVU on the diagonal has double the area of PQRS.
5. Area of SQVU = c × c = c².
6. So c² = 2a².
Answer: c² = 2a², so c = a√2

content.text:
Example 1: Find the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle whose equal sides have length 12.
We have a = 12. Using the formula, we get c = √(2 × 12²) = √288.
We have 16² = 256, and 17² = 289. So, √288 lies between 16 and 17.
The length of the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle, whose length of the equal sides is 12 units, is between 16 and 17 units.
Example 2: If the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle is √72, find its other two sides.
We have c = √72. Using the formula, we get c² = 2a². So, (√72)² = 2a², 72 = 2a². Thus, a² = 72/2 = 36. So, a = √36 = 6.
Therefore, each of the other two sides has length 6.
Use this formula to check your answers to the earlier questions on isosceles right triangles.

content.text:
Finding c from a: square the equal side, double it, and take the square root.
When the root is not a whole number, trap it between the squares of two whole numbers.
Finding a from c: square the hypotenuse, halve it, and take the square root.
The hypotenuse is never the two sides added: 12 + 12 = 24 is far too long.

content.text:
Find the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle whose equal sides have length 12.
1. a = 12.
2. 2 × 12² = 2 × 144 = 288, so c² = 288.
3. c = √288.
4. 16² = 256 and 17² = 289.
5. 256 < 288 < 289, so 16 < √288 < 17.
Answer: c = √288 units, between 16 and 17 units

Use c² = 2a² to check two earlier answers: the hypotenuse for equal sides 3, and the equal sides for hypotenuse 10.
1. Equal sides 3: 2 × 3² = 18, so c = √18.
2. 4² = 16 and 5² = 25, so 4 < √18 < 5, as found by squaring.
3. Hypotenuse 10: 10² = 100, so c² = 100.
4. 100 ÷ 2 = 50, so a² = 50 and each equal side is √50.
Answer: The formula gives √18 and √50, the same answers as before

video_script.anchor: How long is the hypotenuse?
video_script.design: One idea: the area of the square on the hypotenuse comes first, then its side. Assumes: the square on the diagonal of a square has double its area. Wrong idea: the slip adds the two sides. The anchor question stays all video; one hard clear, before the recap.
source: Book question: Find the hypotenuse of the isosceles right triangle whose equal sides are 1 unit
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip adds the two equal sides and says two; a square of side 2 holds 4 unit squares, but the square on the hypotenuse has area 2, so the guess is struck through
maths_rules: The triangle has a right angle; the two sides at the right angle are each 1 unit; the hypotenuse is the side facing the right angle
Two copies of the triangle make the unit square PEAR, side 1: area 1 x 1 = 1 square unit; the hypotenuse ER is its diagonal
The square REST is built on ER; by the doubling rule it has double the area of PEAR: 2 x 1 = 2 square units; REST holds 4 copies of the triangle, PEAR holds 2
The slip's guess 1 + 1 = 2: a square of side 2 has area 2 x 2 = 4 square units, not 2, so the hypotenuse is not 2
If ER = c, then area of REST = c x c = c^2, so c^2 = 2
The number whose square is 2 is written √2 and read root two; c = √2 units
√2 is not placed on a number line in this video; its size is the next concept
your turn: a right triangle with equal sides 2 units; square on a side 2 x 2 = 4, doubled 8, hypotenuse √8 units (never shown)
video_script.payoff_line: The hypotenuse is root two units long

final_answer.value: √2 units
final_answer.spoken: root two units

video_script.substitution: Find the area of the square on the hypotenuse first: it is double the unit square, 2, so the hypotenuse is the length whose square is 2.

media.teaching_notes: The one idea: find the area of the square on the hypotenuse first, then the length whose square is that area. Watch for the slip of adding the two sides to get 2: a square of side 2 has area 4, not 2.

maths_rules: A square has area 2 square units; its side is √2 units
A bigger square has a longer side: of two squares sharing a corner, the one with more area has the longer side
To compare a number with √2, multiply the number by itself and compare the answer with 2
The slip's guess: half of 2 is 1; but 1 x 1 = 1, which is not 2, so √2 is not 1
1 x 1 = 1 and 1 < 2, so the square of side 1 is smaller than the square of area two and 1 < √2
2 x 2 = 4 and 4 > 2, so the square of side 2 is bigger than the square of area two and √2 < 2
So 1 < √2 < 2; 1 is a lower bound and 2 is an upper bound

video_script.design: One idea: the last digit of a square comes from the last digit of the number, and it is never 0. Assumes: multiplying decimals, and 1.414 < root two < 1.415. Wrong idea: the slip trusts the written digits. The anchor question stays all video; one hard clear, before the recap.
source: Book question: If √2 were a terminating decimal of the form 1.414...4, what would be the last digit of its square?

video_script.wrong_move: A common slip trusts the written digits: 1.414213562 ends in 2, and 2 x 2 = 4, so its square ends in 4, not in zeros; it squares to 1.999999998944727844, not 2, and is struck through
maths_rules: The first digits of √2 are 1.414213562
When two decimals are multiplied, the last digit of the answer comes only from their two last digits
Example: 2.3 x 2.3 = 5.29; the last digit 9 comes from 3 x 3 = 9
A decimal that stops has a last digit that is not 0 (a final 0 would be dropped)
The slip's number: 1.414213562 ends in 2; 2 x 2 = 4, so its square ends in 4; 1.414213562 x 1.414213562 = 1.999999998944727844, which is not 2
The book's case: if √2 were 1.414...4, then 4 x 4 = 16, so its square would end in 6: of the form [ ].[ ][ ]...[ ]6
So the square of a stopping decimal never ends in 0 and is never 2.000...; the decimals of √2 go on forever

video_script.design: One idea: count the prime 2 on both sides of 2n squared equals m squared. Assumes: prime factors, and squaring a fraction. maths_rules: A fraction here is m/n with m and n counting numbers (1, 2, 3, ...)
(m/n)^2 = (m x m)/(n x n); m/n = √2 exactly when (m x m)/(n x n) = 2, that is when m x m = 2 x n x n
Case 3/2: m x m = 3 x 3 = 9 and 2 x n x n = 2 x 2 x 2 = 8; 9 is not 8
Case 7/5: 7 x 7 = 49 and 2 x 5 x 5 = 50; 49 is not 50
Square numbers pair their primes: 36 = 6 x 6 = 2 x 3 x 2 x 3 (two 2s, two 3s); 144 = 12 x 12 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 2 x 2 x 3 (four 2s, two 3s)
Given: m and n are counting numbers. To prove: √2 is never equal to m/n. Proof by contradiction
Suppose √2 = m/n; square both sides: 2 = m^2/n^2; multiply both sides by n^2: 2n^2 = m^2
m^2 = m x m, so each 2 in m appears twice: m^2 holds an even number of 2s (0 counts as even)
n^2 holds an even number of 2s; 2n^2 has one more 2, so it holds an odd number of 2s
A counting number splits into primes in only one way, so one number cannot hold both an even and an odd number of 2s; the supposition is false
Conclusion: √2 is not a fraction m/n; this proof is in Euclid's Elements, about 300 BCE, about 2300 years ago
Every stopping decimal is a fraction (such as 0.25 = 25/100), so √2's decimals never stop
Question for the child: for √9, 9n^2 = m^2 has no clash, because 9 = 3 x 3 already holds the prime 3 an even number of times (and √9 = 3 = 3/1)
video_script.payoff_line: Root two is not a fraction

final_answer.value: √2 is not a fraction m/n
final_answer.spoken: root two is not a fraction

Watch for the belief that trying bigger fractions will eventually hit root two: trying can only show misses, a reason covers every fraction at once.

content.text:
Hypotenuse of an Isosceles Right Triangle
Recall that in a right triangle, the side opposite to the right angle is called the hypotenuse.
Find the hypotenuse of this isosceles right triangle.
We know that a square of side 1 unit is made of two such isosceles right triangles. We also know that the square constructed on the diagonal of this square has twice the area of the original square.
We do not yet know the length of the hypotenuse, but we know the area of the square REST on it!
Area of REST = 2 × Area of PEAR = 2 × 1 = 2 sq. units.
We know the relation between the side and the area of a square. If c is the hypotenuse ER, then Area of REST = c × c = c². So, c² = 2. Therefore, c = √2.
Thus, the hypotenuse is of length √2 units.
In the rest of this chapter, we will assume that all the lengths are of a fixed unit unless specified otherwise.

content.text:
The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle. Find the right angle first; the hypotenuse faces it.
Two copies of the triangle make the unit square PEAR, and the hypotenuse ER is its diagonal.
By the doubling rule, the square REST on that diagonal has area 2 × 1 = 2 square units.
A square's area is side × side. So c × c = 2, and the number whose square is 2 is written √2, read 'root two'.
We found the area before the length: squaring turns a length into an area, and the square root turns an area back into a length.

content.text:
Find the hypotenuse of the isosceles right triangle whose equal sides are 1 unit.
1. Two such triangles make the unit square PEAR, of area 1 × 1 = 1 square unit.
2. The hypotenuse ER is the diagonal of PEAR.
3. The square REST on ER has double the area: 2 × 1 = 2 square units.
4. If ER = c, then c × c = 2, so c² = 2.
5. So c = √2.
Answer: √2 units

content.text:
What is the value of √2?
Decimal Representation of √2
The decimal representation of √2 can be found using the following argument.
Is √2 less than or greater than 1?
A square of sidelength 1 unit has an area of 1 sq. unit. A square of sidelength √2 has an area of 2 sq. units. So, 1 is less than √2. In other words, 1² = 1, and √2² = 2. Therefore, 1 < √2.
Is √2 less than or greater than 2?
A square of sidelength 2 units has an area of 4 sq. units. A square of sidelength √2 has an area of 2 sq. units. So, 2 is greater than √2. In other words, √2² = 2, and 2² = 4. Therefore, √2 < 2.
Thus, 1 < √2 < 2.
We call 1 a lower bound on √2 and 2 an upper bound.
Can we find closer bounds for √2?
1.1² = 1.21, 1.2² = 1.44, 1.3² = 1.69, 1.4² = 1.96, 1.5² = 2.25. So, 1.4 < √2 < 1.5
1.41² = 1.9881, 1.42² = 2.0164. So, 1.41 < √2 < 1.42
1.411² = 1.990921, 1.412² = 1.993744, 1.413² = 1.996569, 1.414² = 1.999396, 1.415² = 2.002225. So, 1.414 < √2 < 1.415

content.text:
A bigger square has a bigger side. So to compare a number with √2, compare its square with 2.
1² = 1 is less than 2 and 2² = 4 is more than 2, so 1 < √2 < 2. The number 1 is a lower bound and 2 is an upper bound.
To squeeze closer, square the tenths: 1.4² = 1.96 is just below 2 and 1.5² = 2.25 is above, so 1.4 < √2 < 1.5.
Then square the hundredths between them, then the thousandths. Each round adds one correct digit: 1.414 < √2 < 1.415.

Is √2 less than or greater than 1? Is it less than or greater than 2?
1. 1² = 1, which is less than 2.
2. 2² = 4, which is more than 2.
3. The square of area 2 lies between the squares of areas 1 and 4.
4. So its side lies between 1 and 2.
Answer: 1 < √2 < 2: 1 is a lower bound and 2 an upper bound

content.text:
Will we ever get a number with a terminating decimal representation whose square is 2?
If there is such a terminating decimal starting with 1.414... whose square is 2, then it must have a non-zero last digit. If this is the case, then the decimal representation of its square will also have a non-zero last digit after the decimal point. For example, if √2 is of the form 1.414...4, then its square will be of the form [ ].[ ][ ]...[ ]6
So a terminating decimal cannot have 2 or 2.000... as its square.
Thus, the decimal expansion of √2 must go on forever, i.e., it has a non-terminating decimal representation.
Can √2 be expressed as a fraction m/n, where m and n are counting numbers?
If √2 could be expressed as m/n, then we would have √2 = m/n, 2 = m²/n², 2n² = m².
Recall that in the prime factorization of a square number, each prime occurs an even number of times. So in the equation 2n² = m², the prime 2 would occur an odd number of times on the left side and an even number of times on the right side. This is impossible. Thus √2 cannot be expressed as a fraction m/n.
This beautiful proof that √2 cannot be expressed as m/n where m, n are counting numbers was given by Euclid in his book Elements (c. 300 BCE). We will discuss it in more detail in a later class.
Thus the number √2 cannot be expressed as a terminating decimal or a fraction. But we can think of it as a certain non-terminating decimal: √2 = 1.41421356...

content.text:
Look at the last digit. A decimal that stops has a last digit from 1 to 9, and the last digit of its square is the last digit of that digit's square: 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4 or 1. It is never 0.
So the square of a stopping decimal never ends in zeros and can never be exactly 2.000... The decimals of √2 go on forever.
Could √2 still be a fraction m/n? Then 2n² = m². In a square number every prime appears an even number of times. The right side m² has an even number of 2s; the left side has one more 2 than n², an odd number. One number cannot have both, so √2 is not a fraction.

content.text:
If √2 were a terminating decimal of the form 1.414...4, what would be the last digit of its square?
1. The last digit of the square comes from the last digit of the number.
2. 4 × 4 = 16, so the square ends in 6.
3. A decimal ending in 6 is not 2.000...
4. The same happens for every last digit from 1 to 9: the squares 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81 end in 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4, 1, never in 0.
Answer: 6; no terminating decimal squares to exactly 2

content.text:
Can √2 be expressed as a fraction m/n, where m and n are counting numbers?
1. Suppose √2 = m/n.
2. Square both sides: 2 = m²/n², so 2n² = m².
3. In m², the prime 2 occurs an even number of times.
4. In n² the prime 2 occurs an even number of times, so in 2n² it occurs an odd number of times.
5. One number cannot hold the prime 2 both an even and an odd number of times.
6. So the supposition is impossible.
Answer: No: √2 is not a fraction m/n (Euclid, Elements); √2 = 1.41421356... goes on forever

content.text:
Isosceles Right Triangles, Q2 (i): The length of the two equal sides of an isosceles right triangle is given. Find the length of the hypotenuse. Find bounds on the length of the hypotenuse such that they have at least one digit after the decimal point. (i) 3
1. The square on a side has area 3 × 3 = 9.
2. The square on the hypotenuse has double that area: 2 × 9 = 18.
3. So the hypotenuse is √18.
4. 4² = 16 and 5² = 25, so 4 < √18 < 5.
5. 4.2² = 17.64 and 4.3² = 18.49.
6. So 4.2 < √18 < 4.3.
Answer: √18 units, with 4.2 < √18 < 4.3

content.text:
Isosceles Right Triangles, Q3: The hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle is 10. What are its other two sidelengths? [Hint: Find the area of the square composed of two such right triangles.]
1. Two such triangles make a square whose diagonal is the hypotenuse, 10.
2. The square on the hypotenuse has area 10 × 10 = 100.
3. The square made of the two triangles has half that area: 100 ÷ 2 = 50.
4. Its side is an equal side of the triangle, so each equal side is √50.
5. 7² = 49 and 8² = 64, so 7 < √50 < 8.
6. 7.07² = 49.9849 and 7.08² = 50.1264, so 7.07 < √50 < 7.08.
Answer: Each of the other two sides is √50, between 7.07 and 7.08
facts: 2.3 FiO3: equal side squared and two-decimal bounds
steps: Two such triangles make a square whose diagonal is the hypotenuse, 10.
The square on the hypotenuse has area 10 × 10 = 100.
The square made of the two triangles has half that area: 100 ÷ 2 = 50.
Its side is an equal side of the triangle, so each equal side is √50.
content.answer: Each of the other two sides is √50, between 7.07 and 7.08

Teaching purpose: The square on the hypotenuse, T + U + V, and the two joined squares, V + W + X, are made of the same piece V and two copies of one right triangle, so they have the same area.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: teal #0072B2 for the first set, amber #E69F00 for the second set, green #009E73 for what agrees or works, reddish purple #CC79A7 for the focus, grey #6B7280 for construction; muted red #D55E00 only for a wrong or impossible case, never as decoration. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. Two figures side by side with an arrow from left to right. Left: the tilted square split into T, U and V. Right: the two joined squares split into W, V and X. T, U, W and X filled teal, V filled amber in both, the same size and position in both figures. Thin dark outlines.

Exact mathematical structure:
- Drawing units with a = 2 and b = 3, both figures at the same scale.
- Left figure: tilted square with corners (0, 2), (3, 0), (5, 3), (2, 5); T is (0, 2), (2, 2), (2, 5); U is (2, 5), (2, 3), (5, 3); V is (0, 2), (2, 2), (2, 3), (5, 3), (3, 0).
- Right figure: small square (0, 0) to (2, 2) joined to large square (2, 0) to (5, 3); W is (0, 2), (0, 0), (3, 0); X is (3, 0), (5, 0), (5, 3); V is the same five-sided piece in the same place.
- One arrow from the left figure to the right figure.
- Each piece carries its letter, once, inside it.

Visible text:
- T
- U
- V
- W
- X

Critical rejection conditions:
- V drawn a different shape or size in the two figures
- T, U, W and X not all congruent
- the tilted square not a true square
- any area values, equations or words in the frame
- any count of objects, cells, ticks or dots that differs from the numbers stated above
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
- a right angle drawn visibly different from 90 degrees, or a right-angle mark on a corner that is not a right angle

Student takeaway: Swap two copies of the triangle for two others and the area stays the same.

video_script.anchor: Why are all four sides of T + U + V equal?
video_script.design: One idea: each side is the hypotenuse of a copy of one right triangle. Assumes: Baudhāyana's rule and the word perpendicular sides. Wrong idea: taking a + b as the side. The joined squares with T, U, V, W and X stay on stage from the hook to the idea; one clear before the recap.
source: Book question: Why are all four sides of the 4-sided figure T + U + V equal?
never_show: a side labelled a + b (only struck through)
video_script.wrong_move: The slip says each side is a + b, the two squares' sides together; the bottom edge, which is a + b long, is laid along a tilted side and runs far past its end.
maths_rules: drawing units a = 2, b = 3, bottom left corner at (0,0); small square (0,0) to (2,2); big square (2,0) to (5,3); the figure is for any a < b, and no numbers are shown
the marked point is (3,0), a distance a from the right end; the bottom edge splits into a, b - a, a
X: (3,0), (5,0), (5,3), right angle at (5,0), perpendicular sides a (along the bottom) and b (up the right side)
W: (0,2), (0,0), (3,0), right angle at (0,0), perpendicular sides a (up) and a + (b - a) = b (along the bottom)
T: (0,2), (2,2), (2,5), right angle at (2,2); U: (2,5), (2,3), (5,3), right angle at (2,3); each has perpendicular sides a and b
V is the five-sided middle piece (0,2), (2,2), (2,3), (5,3), (3,0); the tilted figure is (0,2), (3,0), (5,3), (2,5) = T + U + V
T, U, W and X are right triangles with the same two perpendicular sides a and b, so they are congruent and their hypotenuses are equal, length c
the four sides of the figure are the hypotenuses of W (bottom left), X (bottom right), U (top right) and T (top left); each is c (in drawing units, √13)
The slipped a + b is the whole bottom edge, 5 drawing units, longer than a tilted side of √13, which is between 3 and 4
your turn: squares of sides 2 and 7; the middle part of the bottom edge is 7 - 2 = 5; never shown
video_script.payoff_line: each side is the hypotenuse of a congruent right triangle, so all four sides are c

final_answer.value: Each side is the hypotenuse of a congruent right triangle, so all four sides equal c

T, U, W and X are congruent right triangles with perpendicular sides a and b, so each has area a x b ÷ 2 (3 in drawing units)
W turns a quarter turn anticlockwise about (0,2), the top left corner of the small square, and lands exactly on T: (0,0) goes to (2,2) and (3,0) goes to (2,5)
X turns a quarter turn clockwise about (5,3), the top right corner of the big square, and lands exactly on U: (3,0) goes to (2,5) and (5,0) goes to (2,3)
V never moves; turning a piece does not change its area; so T + U + V = V + W + X

media.title: Four equal sides: why is every corner a right angle?
media.context: Class 8 'The Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem'. Worked video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea.
media.description: The tilted figure T + U + V has four equal sides, but a rhombus has those too. The video asks whether every corner of the figure is a right angle, and tests the idea using the sharp angles of the right triangles.

in each right triangle T, U, W, X one angle is 90; call the sharp angle facing the side a x; the angles add to 180, so the other sharp angle is 180 - 90 - x = 90 - x
bottom corner (3,0): W brings x, X brings 90 - x, both on the straight bottom edge (180); corner = 180 - x - (90 - x) = 90
top corner (2,5): T brings x, U brings 90 - x; corner = x + (90 - x) = 90
left corner (0,2): the small square's corner is 90; W takes 90 - x, leaving x inside V; T adds 90 - x; corner = x + (90 - x) = 90
right corner (5,3): the big square's corner is 90; X takes x, leaving 90 - x inside V; U adds x; corner = (90 - x) + x = 90
four sides c and four right angles make a square

your turn: x = 35; the other sharp angle is 90 - 35 = 55; at the top corner 35 + 55 = 90; never shown

maths_rules: drawing units a = 2 and b = 3 (any a smaller than b works); small square (0,0) to (2,2), big square (2,0) to (5,3), joined along the bottom, small square on the left
the bottom edge is a + b = 5 long; the cut point P is (3,0): a = 2 from the right end, b = 3 from the left end, b - a = 1 from the join

cut 1 runs from P (3,0) to (0,2), the top left corner of the small square; the left piece is the triangle (0,0), (3,0), (0,2) with legs b = 3 and a = 2 and its right angle at (0,0); cut 1 has length √13 = c

cut 2 runs from P (3,0) to (5,3), the top right corner of the big square; the right piece is the triangle (3,0), (5,0), (5,3) with legs a = 2 and b = 3 and its right angle at (5,0); cut 2 has length √13 = c
both side pieces are the same right triangle (legs a and b), so both cuts have the same length c
the middle piece (0,2), (2,2), (2,3), (5,3), (3,0) stays still
the left triangle turns a quarter turn anticlockwise about (0,2) and lands on (0,2), (2,2), (2,5); the right triangle turns a quarter turn clockwise about (5,3) and lands on (2,5), (2,3), (5,3)
the new shape has corners (0,2), (3,0), (5,3), (2,5): four sides of length √13 = c and four right angles, so it is a square of side c
area check: 4 + 9 = 13 = (√13)², that is a² + b² = c²; no piece is stretched, so the area stays a² + b²

area: the pieces are only moved, so the new shape has area a² + b²; it is a square of side c, area c²; so a² + b² = c²

video_script.anchor: A square of side a: how do you build a square with 3 times its area? With 5 times?
video_script.design: One idea: to build a square of a chosen area, choose the right triangle whose leg squares add up to it. Assumes: the diagonal square is double, and the theorem. Wrong idea: tripling the side. The given square stays in the anchor band all video; one clear, before the recap.

video_script.wrong_move: The slip triples the side. A square of side 3a holds 9 copies of the given square, not 3; the 3 by 3 grid of copies shows it.
maths_rules: the given square has side a and area a²
its diagonal d satisfies d² = a² + a² = 2a², so the square on the diagonal has double the area
triple: a right triangle with legs a and d has hypotenuse h with h² = a² + d² = a² + 2a² = 3a²
five times: two sides laid end to end make 2a, and (2a)² = 4a²; a right triangle with legs a and 2a has hypotenuse k with k² = a² + 4a² = 5a²

content.text:
Combining Two Different Squares
We have seen in the previous sections how to combine two copies of the same square to make a larger square whose area is the sum of the areas of the two smaller squares.
The sidelength of the larger square is the length of the diagonal of either of the smaller squares.
What if we wish to combine two squares of 'different' sizes to make a large square whose area is the sum of the two smaller squares?
In his Śulba-Sūtra (Verse 1.12), Baudhāyana also gives a truly remarkable solution to this more general problem of combining two different sized squares. He writes:
The area of the square produced by the diagonal is the sum of the areas of the squares produced by the two sides.
That is, to combine two different squares, make a right-angled triangle whose perpendicular sides are the sidelengths of the two squares. The square whose sidelength is the hypotenuse of this right-angled triangle has an area that is the sum of the areas of the original two squares.
Can you see why the method works in the case where the two squares are the same size? Does it agree with the method we used earlier to combine two same sized squares into a bigger square?

content.text:
Two equal squares combine into the square on the diagonal of either one.
For two different squares, Baudhāyana's rule is: put their sides at a right angle to make a right triangle; the square on its hypotenuse has the combined area.
Areas 9 and 16 have sides 3 and 4. The square on the hypotenuse of the right triangle with sides 3 and 4 has area 9 + 16 = 25, so its side is 5, not 3 + 4 = 7.
When the two squares are equal, the right triangle has two equal sides: it is half of one square, its hypotenuse is that square's diagonal, and the rule gives the doubling method again.

Can you see why the method works when the two squares are the same size? Does it agree with the earlier method?
1. Two equal squares have side a.
2. The right triangle with both perpendicular sides a is half of one square, cut along its diagonal.

content.text:
Why does Baudhāyana's method work?
Subsequently in his Śulba-Sūtra (Verse 2.1), Baudhāyana provides another verse that helps in explaining why the method works in general:
To combine different squares, mark a rectangular portion of the larger square using a side of the smaller square. The diagonal of this rectangle is the side of a square that has area equal to the sum of the areas of the smaller squares.
Let us follow Baudhayan's instructions.
Join the two squares.
Mark a rectangular portion of the larger square using a side of the smaller one, and draw its diagonal. By doing this, we get a right triangle with perpendicular sides a and b.
Make a 4-sided figure over the hypotenuse by drawing three more of such right triangles:
The 4-sided figure obtained (T + U + V) is in fact a square with an area equal to the sum of the areas of the two smaller squares!
Why?
As T, U, X and W are all congruent, the sides of this new 4-sided figure all have the same length. Notice the angles.
Explain why all the angles of this new 4-sided figure are right angles and so it is a square.
Notice that this new square has as its sidelength, the hypotenuse of the right triangle of sides a and b.
Baudhāyana's assertion is now clear:
The area of the square on the hypotenuse = the sum of the areas of T, U, and V = the sum of the areas of V, W, and X = the sum of the areas of the two given squares.

Step 2: inside the big square, mark a rectangle a wide and b tall at its right end. Its diagonal gives a right triangle X with perpendicular sides a and b.

content.text:
Explain Baudhāyana's assertion: the square on the hypotenuse has the same area as the two given squares.
1. The square on the hypotenuse is made of T, U and V.
2. The two given squares, joined, are made of V, W and X.
3. T, U, W and X are congruent, so T and U together have the same area as W and X together.
4. So T + U + V has the same area as V + W + X.
5. Moving W and X to the places of T and U turns the two squares into the square on the hypotenuse.
Answer: Square on the hypotenuse = T + U + V = V + W + X = the two given squares

content.text:
Explain why all the angles of this new 4-sided figure are right angles and so it is a square.
1. In the right triangle with sides a and b, call one acute angle x; the angles add to 180 and one is 90, so the other acute angle is 90 − x.
2. At the corner on the bottom edge, the angle x of W and the angle 90 − x of X lie on the straight edge on either side of the corner, so the corner is 180 − x − (90 − x), which is 90.
3. At each of the other three corners, an angle x and an angle 90 − x together make the corner: x + (90 − x), which is 90.
4. Four equal sides and four right angles make a square.
Answer: Every corner is a right angle and every side is c, so the figure is a square on the hypotenuse

content.text:
Combining Two Squares Using Paper
Cut out and join two different sized squares as follows:
Now make two cuts to make three pieces:
Rearrange the three pieces into a larger square:
You have now combined two smaller squares into a larger square!
Now make a right triangle using the two smaller squares. Draw a square on the hypotenuse.
Cover the square on the hypotenuse using your pieces.
This shows that if a right triangle has shorter sides of length a and b, and hypotenuse of length c, then the areas of the two smaller squares, a² and b², add up to the area of the larger square, c²: a² + b² = c².
This is the famous and fundamental theorem of Baudhāyana on right-angled triangles:
Baudhāyana's Theorem on Right-angled triangles: If a right-angled triangle has sidelengths a, b, and c, where c is the length of the hypotenuse, then a² + b² = c².
Baudhāyana was the first person in history to state this theorem in this generality and essentially modern form. The theorem is also known as the Pythagorean Theorem, after the Greek philosopher-mathematician Pythagoras (c. 500 BCE) who also admired and studied this theorem, and lived a couple hundred years after Baudhāyana. It is also often called the transitional name 'Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem' so that everyone knows what theorem is being referred to.

Join a square of side a to a square of side b. Mark the point on the bottom edge that is a from the right end.
Cut from that point to the top-left corner of the small square and to the top-right corner of the large square: three pieces, two of them right triangles with sides a and b and hypotenuse c.
Turn the two triangles a quarter turn about the outer top corners; the three pieces make one square with side c.
Now make a right triangle with the two squares on its sides and cover the square on its hypotenuse with the three pieces: nothing is left over and nothing is missing.
So a² + b² = c². The theorem holds only when the angle between a and b is a right angle, and c is always the side opposite that angle.

content.text:
Combine two squares of sides a and b using paper: make two cuts, get three pieces, and rearrange them into one square.
1. Join the squares side by side along their bottoms, the square of side a on the left.
2. Mark the point on the bottom edge at distance a from the right end; it is b − a from the join.
3. Cut from that point to the top-left corner of the small square: this cut has length c.
4. Cut from the same point to the top-right corner of the large square: this cut also has length c.
5. Turn each right triangle a quarter turn about the outer top corner it shares with the squares: the three pieces make one square of side c.
Answer: One square of side c, whose area is a² + b²

State Baudhāyana's theorem on right-angled triangles, and say why it has two names.

content.text:
Missing Sides and New Squares, Q3: Using the constructions you have now seen, how would you construct a square whose area is triple the area of a given square? Five times the area of a given square? (Baudhāyana's Śulba-Sūtra, Verse 1.10)
1. Let the given square have side a and area a².
2. Its diagonal d is the side of the square with double the area: d² = 2a².
3. Make a right triangle with perpendicular sides a and d.
4. The square on its hypotenuse has area a² + 2a² = 3a²: triple.
5. For five times, make a right triangle with perpendicular sides a and 2a.
6. The square on its hypotenuse has area a² + 4a² = 5a².
Answer: Triple: the square on the hypotenuse of the right triangle whose sides are a side and a diagonal of the given square. Five times: the square on the hypotenuse of the right triangle with sides a and 2a

4. The square on that third side has area 24 square units.
Answer: The square on the third side of the right triangle with hypotenuse 7 and one side 5: area 24 square units

1. The areas are 7² = 49 and 5² = 25, and 49 − 25 = 24.
2. Draw a side of 5 units, a right angle at one end, and swing an arc of radius 7 from the other end to meet the perpendicular: a right triangle with hypotenuse 7 and one side 5.
3. Its third side b has b² = 7² − 5², which is 24.
4. The square on that third side has area 24 square units.
Answer: The square on the third side of the right triangle with hypotenuse 7 and one side 5: area 24 square units

Side labels sit outside each triangle, next to the side they name.

Exact mathematical structure:

- Left (upright): the right angle at the bottom left; the 3 cm side vertical, the 4 cm side horizontal along the bottom, the 5 cm hypotenuse sloping down from the top of the 3 cm side to the right end of the 4 cm side.
